tip: 얼굴이 작아요 (eolgur-i jagayo = 'the face is small') is a compliment – a small face is a Korean beauty ideal, so this is praise for the actor.
마음 (maeum) means heart and mind at once, so 마음이 따뜻해요 (maeum-i ttatteutaeyo) praises someone's whole inner self as warm, not just their feelings.
닮았어요 (dalmasseoyo) is past tense for a present fact – Korean treats resemblance as settled long ago: you took after Dad once, and it stuck.
그분 (geubun), the respectful 'that person', pulls the verb up with it: 계세요 (gyeseyo) is the honorific 'is (somewhere)', replacing plain 있어요 (isseoyo).
살 (sal) counts age with native numbers: 몇 살이에요? (myeot sar-ieyo? = how old are you?)
스물 (seumul = twenty) shrinks to 스무 (seumu) before a counter: 스무 살 (seumu sal = twenty years). Korean numbers slim down to count, like 하나 (hana) becoming 한 (han).
나이가 많아요 (nai-ga manayo) is literally 'age is many' – Korean stacks up years instead of calling someone old, and it works for dogs too.
나이가 어떻게 돼요? (nai-ga eotteoke dwaeyo?) is the soft way to ask an age, roughly 'how does your age turn out?' – 몇 살이에요? (myeot sarieyo?) is the blunt version, fine for kids.
축하해요 (chukahaeyo = congratulations) follows the occasion word: 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukahaeyo) = birthday congratulations. Swap the occasion, keep the ending.
-들 (deul) makes plurals: 친구들 (chingu-deul = friends). Korean often skips it.
처음 뵙겠습니다 (cheoeum boepgetseumnida) is the set formal line for a first meeting – literally 'I meet you for the first time' – so it only fits the first time you meet someone.
이쪽은 (ijjogeun) introduces a person as 'this side is...' – gesturing toward a direction rather than at the person is a polite Korean way to introduce someone.
이분 (ibun), the respectful 'this person', lifts the verb ending too: 어머니세요 (eomeoni-seyo), not plain 어머니예요 (eomeoni-yeyo) – respected subjects take -세요 (-seyo).
어디에서 왔어요? (eodieseo wasseoyo?) is literally 'where did you come from?' – Korean asks about origin in the past tense, as a completed journey.
잘 지내요? (jal jinaeyo?) is literally 'are you getting along well?' – 지내다 (jinaeda) means to spend your days, so you're asking how life is passing.
마셔요 (masyeoyo) can be a statement, a question, or 'let's drink' – one polite form covers all three. 같이 (gachi = together) is the clue this one is an invitation.
시 hours take native numbers: 일곱 시 (ilgop si = 7 o'clock).
로 (ro) marks your means of transport: 지하철로 (jihacheol-lo) = by subway. Other vehicles work the same way – 버스로 (beoseu-ro = by bus), 차로 (cha-ro = by car).
갈아타요 (garatayo) is built from 갈다 (galda = change) + 타다 (tada = ride) – transferring between lines is literally 'change-riding'.
분 minutes take Sino numbers: 사십 분 (sasip bun = 40 minutes).
길이 막혀요 (giri makyeoyo) is literally 'the road is blocked' – Korean describes a traffic jam from the road's point of view, not the traffic's.
퇴근 시간 (toegeun sigan) = 'leaving-work time' = the evening rush hour.
부터 (buteo) glues straight onto a time word: 다음 주부터 (daeum ju-buteo) = starting next week. Its endpoint partner is 까지 (kkaji = until).
출근길 (chulgeungil) = the way to work; -길 (gil) makes 'route' words.
우리 회사 (uri hoesa) is 'our company' even when the listener works somewhere else – 우리 (uri) covers whatever you belong to: company, school, house.
At work Koreans normally use title + 님 (nim): 과장님 (gwajangnim = manager + respect ending). A colleague's bare name can sound rude, so the title itself is the polite address.
중 (jung) after a noun means 'in the middle of it': 출장 중 (chuljang jung) = mid-business-trip. Other activity nouns work too – 회의 중 (hoei jung) = in a meeting.
-세요 (-seyo) adds respect for the boss: 회의 중이세요 (hoei jung-iseyo = is in a meeting).
안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) is literally 'it doesn't become' – the all-purpose Korean for 'it's not working', whether it's a computer, a plan, or a request.
께 (kke) is the honorific 'to': 부장님께 (bujangnimkke) = to the department head. With friends it's plain 한테 (hante) – same job, no deference.
